en: Chapter 9 (untitled). 35.
Total: 103 verses.
TY_1.1ab: The lion to the serpent of thick darkness, the sovereign of the abode of the three worlds, the eye of the world;
Victorious is the sun, the crest-jewel and sole ornament of the sky.

With my head, I bow to Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī, together with the world-protectors and the Supreme Lord; to the Lotus-born Brahmā, the Lotus-wealth Viṣṇu, and Hari, the Sun who is the lamp of the three worlds.
From this point forward is the rule for the expedition of one desiring victory, whose time of birth is known.

When the hour and the zodiacal sign are known, when the positional strength of the planets has been grasped, and when the lifespan has been fully determined, then the auspicious or inauspicious result may be declared.
Thus, the instruction of the treatise concerns a contradiction with what has been introduced regarding a settled subject;
some speak of the time of birth, while many others do not.
If, at the time of the query, the birth asterism and the ascendant of the rising sign coincide with those of the two persons desiring to march,
or if the rising signs are the third, sixth, eleventh, or the head (the tenth), and the paths are favorable, there shall be victory.
The ascendant or the sign of the enemy, its lord, the natal sign, or its lord [are the factors to be considered].
If [the Moon] is situated in the hibuka, even so, it should be declared that the enemy has been slain.
When the question is pleasing, the sight of auspicious objects is recommended;
if the querent asks with reverence, the astrologer should predict victory.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Vijayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā yield fruits corresponding to their names;
these lunar days (tithis) are most auspicious when increasing or equal in duration during the bright fortnight, while in the dark fortnight, they have the opposite effect.
The scattering of rays from the clusters of stars, their being overtaken by the twilight, their being pierced by planets,
their being oppressed by cruel [planets], and their being defiled by portents— all such things are inauspicious.
The remaining asterisms are auspicious for vehicles, though they do not bestow excessive merit.
For one desiring to burn the territory of an enemy, the auspicious Āgneyī [nakṣatra] is favorable until sunrise;
however, it is not so during the forenoon on days when Viśākhā, Rohiṇī, or the Uttarās are present.
One should avoid traveling at midday under the asterisms Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and Ārdrā;
one should avoid traveling in the afternoon under Svātī, Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Hasta.

One should set out at nightfall under the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Citrā, and Revatī; or under the first three asterisms of the southern quarter (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā) and Pitrya (Maghā), avoiding the middle of the night.
Not during the latter part of the night, nor under the asterisms of Punarvasu or the three beginning with Śraviṣṭhā (Vaiṣṇava).
All times are auspicious under Śravaṇa, Jyeṣṭhā (Indra), Hasta, and Puṣya.
The seven constellations beginning with Kṛttikā are situated in order starting from the east and so forth;
they follow the natural sequence, and there is unity between the eastern and northern hips.
Those who, having crossed the line in the direction of fire and wind known as the *parigha*,
fall before long into calamity, as if by the command of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The four lunar mansions beginning with Sarvadvārika have been designated;
they are Puṣya, Hasta, Aśvinī, and the mansion whose deity is Mitra.
Jyeṣṭhā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Rohiṇī, and Uttaraphalgunī are the "tridents" (śūla) in the eastern and subsequent directions; if [the moon] passes through them, it is a portentous marvel (citram).
The *tārā* [stars] bring about birth, prosperity, misfortune, security, ruin, auspiciousness, and hardship;
these are designated as "friendly" (*maitra*) or "exceedingly friendly" (*atimaitra*), and they yield fruits corresponding to those designations.
On Sunday, there is loss of wealth; on Monday, a decline in strength and loss of food;
on Tuesday, diseases of fire, blood, and bile; and on Wednesday, the acquisition of friends.

During the day of Saturn, there is gain of life, victory, and wealth; under Venus, there is the acquisition of women, clothing, perfumes, and riches; yet one also encounters wretchedness, imprisonment, and disease.
Success for those setting out occurs on a day when the planets are in a state of accumulation (*upacaya*), even if they are malefic;
however, even if the planets are benefic, if they are not situated in a state of accumulation, the journey will not be auspicious for the traveler. [Regarding *viṣṭi*...]
The unfavorable astrological configurations (karaṇas) are avoided for one who sets out on a journey;
however, some authorities permit even the *gara* configuration for merchants when engaged in mercantile activities.
Indra, Agni, Niśācara, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Ayoṇi arise during the day.
Rudra, Ahibudhnya, Pūṣan, Dakṣa, Antaka, Agni, Dhātṛ,
Indra, Aditi, Guru, Hari, Āditya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Anila— these are the names of the moments (kṣaṇas) during the night.
A fifteenth part of the day and likewise of the night is designated as a *muhūrta*.
This should be understood by those who know it through the application of shadows, water-clocks, and other instruments.
Like the constellations, the *parigha* and other [omens] of the moments should be considered together with their presiding deities.
That very same result has been observed by Garga and others; and regarding this, there are verses: [The verses follow.]
A full day and night, joined with the moon and the lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
as well as those specific nakṣatras and muhūrtas, are traditionally held to possess equal karmic qualities.
And that which is the eighth muhūrta, named Viriñci, is designated as Abhijit;
in that [muhūrta], for one who has gone beyond the three [worlds] toward the southern direction, there is the attainment of victory.
On the eighth day, when it is even, there is an auspicious moment known as Viriñcivibhu;
by that [moment], the vehicle was abandoned toward the south in all directions.
The Moon, when victorious, is praised;
it is auspicious when situated in the seventh house from the house of accumulation (the second), even if it is in the natal sign during a journey.
Or, when conjoined with a productive [planet] in the midst of benefics, it brings about auspiciousness.
The Moon is not desired even when situated in the third, sixth, eleventh, or seventh house; however, it yields desirable results when it possesses four or two *vedhas*.

At the beginning of the bright fortnight, when the moon is auspicious, the fortnight is auspicious; when it is inauspicious, it is inauspicious. In the dark fortnight, it is auspicious if it grants a favorable range (*gocara*); otherwise, it is not auspicious even during the bright fortnight.
The ascendant at one's birth is desired, not the rising of the birth-sign; from the positions of those two,
the third and eleventh houses are beneficial, while the others are not desired at the time of rising.
When the combust Mars is in the sixth house, there is the destruction of the enemy; when it is in the ascendant, there is the death of the traveler.
Some wicked people sang thus when they were in a place of distress.
In the zodiac signs during the current birth, those which are occupied by benefics, the Sun, or Venus—
These are commended for the ascendant; evil planets are not desired there.

In ascendants that rise with their heads [pointing upward], there is victory; in ascendants that rise with their sixth parts [pointing upward], there is defeat. In those that rise with their directions [pointing upward], there is victory; in those that rise with their openings [pointing upward], there is defeat in battle.
In Pisces, the path is crooked; that same [crookedness] occurs when the Moon is in the ascendant.
Travel by boat is the activity associated with a watery ascendant, or it may occur when the Moon is in its ninth-part (navāṃśa).
With his nine limbs withered like a decaying tree, he stood dejected among the cruel [planets],
like a wise man in his final days, tormented by the indulgences of youth.
Prosperity comes to one desiring to travel when auspicious planets are situated in the nine limbs of the ascendant,
just as those possessing merit attain the forest of youth through skillful means.
In a gentle nine-limbed ascendant, it produces an unassailable enjoyment of the enemy's strength;
whatever its fruit is during the day, that remains in its entirety during the *kālahorā*.
Even for a cruel [planet], a group of planets that produces accumulation is praised when situated in the ascendant;
[this is also true] when the Moon is joined with a quarter [of its strength].
And [the mantra] of the gentle Lord of the Tantra.
Thus, one should avoid malefic planets situated in the eighth house,
as well as the eighth house itself and the ascendant.
And when the Moon is situated in Nidhana, it is unfavorable for the undertaking of all enterprises.
A journey undertaken without the *lagna* (ascendant) is like a woman who has lost her husband;
having reached the month of her birth, she goes to destruction.
Gradually, little by little.
Whatever conduct a woman of noble family maintains through her very character, her virtues are carried away by it, just as the most excellent forms are captivated by beauty. E7

When benefic planets are situated in the ascendant, there is good health and happiness of mind; when they are situated in the second house, there is an accumulation of wealth; and when they are situated in the third house, there is an increase in kinsmen.
Through planets situated in the fourth house, there is an increase in vehicles and friends; through those in the fifth, there is the strength of ministers.
Through those in the sixth, there is the destruction of enemies; and in the seventh houses, all are beneficial except for Venus.
In the first, fourth, seventh, eighth, and ninth houses, there is protection of life, wealth, and— excluding the fourth— a treasury;
in the tenth house and those following it, there is success in action, gain, and the attainment of strength.
If Mars, the Sun, Saturn, and the Moon are in the ascendant, there will be killing, imprisonment, death, and terror;
if they are in the second house, there is loss of wealth; if situated in the third house, there is fame and splendor.
Separation from vehicles and kinsmen, loss of one's mantra, and the destruction of enemies—
these occur when the seventh house from Hihuka and the other houses is occupied by Saturn, resulting in the ruin of one's own domain.

Death occurs when [the lords] have reached their destruction; a great calamity for the army occurs when they are situated in the ninth house. Mars and the Sun situated in the tenth house grant victory, while Saturn brings about defeat.

Victory is achieved when malefic planets are situated in the eleventh house and the final houses (twelfth and seventh), provided they do not lose their own strength; with benefics in the same positions—excluding the houses of increase (the third, sixth, and eleventh)—there is success for the traveler. With malefics, the result is the reverse.
Even a cruel planet situated in its favorable sign is auspicious when placed in the ascendant, whereas even an auspicious one is undesirable there if it is retrograde.
A retrograde planet is not auspicious in a quadrant; likewise applies that day and the ascendant belonging to its own division.
The lords of the Sāman chants are Jupiter and the Sun; Rāhu, Ketu, Mercury, and Saturn are the lords of dissension; the Sun and Mars are the lords of punishment; and the Moon is the lord of bestowal.
Success is achieved through the ruler, enemies, ministers, the crown prince, guild leaders, laborers, and lords of valor,
as well as by favorable planets such as the Sun and others belonging to those respective divisions.
When the planets are situated in their debilitated signs, overcome by other planets, eclipsed by the Sun, devoid of rays, and diminished,
they become incapable of performing their functions in the ascendant, like serpents subdued by mantras.
Those for whom the benefics are situated in the ninth, fifth, or seventh houses during their transit, while the malefics are located in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses,
return to their own abodes having accomplished their purpose, provided that the gifts have been duly bestowed upon the twice-born according to the prescribed rules.
If there is not even a single benefic planet in a quadrant during the time of departure,
whether in the birth chart or in the tenth house (the house of action), the teachers say that such a journey is not auspicious.
Rāhu, the Sun, Ketu, and Venus are known as "marchers" (yāyin), while the Moon, Jupiter, Mercury, and Saturn are "citizens" (paura); furthermore, the Sun is also a citizen during the forenoon.
Accompanied by those traveling with him who are well-disposed, and having taken leave of the citizens while seated,
he should proceed with half of his army, even if accompanied by other auspicious non-citizens.
Even when all [planets] are inauspicious, one should resort to a preeminent king whose destiny is auspicious;

for there is the accomplishment of power through strong benefics, and victory in battle through strong malefics. Traveling in accordance with the solstice (ayana) is beneficial when both the Sun and the Moon are not in conjunction.
Day and night one should march for victory; in the opposite case, there will be the destruction and defeat of the afflictions.
From whichever direction Venus has risen during its revolution, or in whichever of its courses it moves, a planet rising in that same direction is called *pratiśukra* (opposed to Venus);
its rising there must be avoided with great effort.
When Venus is retrograde, not even the slightest purpose of those who travel succeeds;
one who wishes to live may go against Venus at will, but never when Venus has set.
When Venus is turbid, afflicted by a planet, retrograde, heliacally set, or situated in its sign of debilitation,
even a king endowed with full strength who has marched against the enemy falls under the enemy's power.
The planet Mars causes fear of fire, brings about the destruction of the treasury,
and leads to victory over enemies.
The son of the Moon (Mercury) [causes] the destruction of the army and elephants;
Jupiter [causes] death; the son of the Sun (Saturn) [causes] the destruction of men and kings;
and the king of Brahmins (Jupiter) [causes] the destruction of wealth.
All these,
together with Bhārgava, were indeed the foremost ministers of the enemy of the gods (Śukra), who was born of Atri.
The lunar mansion, the lunar day, as well as the *karaṇa*, the day of the week, the planetary transit, and the *navāṃśa*.

Whether it be the day of the planet, the ascendant, or even the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), as well as all other favorable omens (*śakuna*) and so forth that have been described— they are all auspicious.
At that time, even the preceptor of the descendant of Bhṛgu did not live longer than his own life-span.
Even a powerful king,
if he sets out while thirsting for victory in battle, having placed the priest at his back, shall conquer his enemies.
Having gratified the earth with the blood of his enemies' armies,
he enjoys it for a long time, possessing far-reaching and vast fame.
Like a boat with a rudder out of order,
like a bride whose husband has died, and like the sky when the sun has set— so does she wander.
Or where the crops have perished and the clouds are devoid of semen (rain), that is the place.
Even in such a situation, if Mercury is favorably situated in relation to Venus,
no other planets are capable of rescuing one who has been overtaken by the adverse influence of Rahu.
One should not travel toward that direction in which one's husband resides, nor when he is situated there;
one should proceed only when the lord of that direction is favorable and has passed beyond the thorns.
Through theft, assault, falsehood, and battle, they meet with failure.
Having offered oblations into the fire, paid homage to the deities, and caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings,
the king, with a serene mind, should proceed without delay while meditating upon the guardian of the direction.

Some teachers say that he went there of his own accord due to the exigency of the task; indeed, upon his departure, one should employ the royal umbrella, weapons, and other auspicious, victory-bringing items.
When there is thunder,
one should somehow maintain composure;
likewise, for up to seven days, one should remain steady amidst divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
The throbbing of the right side is auspicious, excluding the heart and the back; so too is the purity of intention and the arrival of news. And this verse was spoken by the sages:
When all signs, whether auspicious or inauspicious, are gathered on one side,
and the mind goes toward another side alone, that is pure and brings victory.
When the king has mounted, if a horse that follows the procession, being well-trained,
neighs toward another horse or touches its own right side with its mouth, that horse will soon increase the prosperity of its master.
If a horse repeatedly voids urine and excrement even when being beaten, does not move in the proper direction,
is fearful of what ought not to be done, and has tearful eyes, it portends no good for its master.

With a faltering gait, his ears suddenly bristling with alarm, he is exceedingly dejected and pants softly and deeply; with his forelegs cast upon the ground, his eyes are rapidly closed, he is prone to sleep, devoid of vigor, causing fear, and eating unwholesome things; and not once does he fail to discharge blood and excrement.
Crushing anthills, stumps, thickets, grass, and trees at will with a joyful gaze,
it should proceed in the direction of the march with quick steps, holding its head high;
and when the time for girthing and saddling arrives, it should either emit a great spray of saliva or trumpet loudly.
Or at that time, upon attaining intoxication, one who brings victory should then bite the right tusk while encircling it.
White mustard seeds, a mirror, milk, and collyrium; a bound animal, meat, and a full jar;
curd, honey, ghee, yellow pigment (rocanā), and young maidens; a banner, gold, a lotus, a noble throne, and a conch shell;
a white bull, flowers, and garments; fish, a flock of birds, courtesans, and trusted people dressed in beautiful attire.
There were fruits of flaming fire, uncut sugarcane, and food; weapons such as elephants, drums, goads, and chowries;
and various kinds of jewels, foremost among them emeralds, rubies, sapphires, and crystals.
Whether auspicious signs are produced spontaneously or proclaimed without effort,
he conquers the entire earth by means of their being perceived, seen, touched, or heard.

Cotton, medicinal herbs, black grain, salt, eunuchs, bones, oil, fat, mud, charcoal, molasses, snakes, hides, and excrement— these, as well as those afflicted by disease, are inauspicious. So too are those with shaven heads, those smeared with unguents, those with disheveled hair, outcasts, and those wearing saffron robes.

One should take a path that resounds with the sharp sounds of paṭaha, mṛdaṅga, conchs, bherīs, and paṇavas; adorned with banners and the tops of archways; where the dust is laid by an abundance of flowers and water; and frequented by people who are fragrant and well-attired.

Whatever auspicious or inauspicious signs have been prescribed here for those departing, those same favorable or unfavorable omens apply even in dreams; furthermore, being smeared with excrement is auspicious.
A gentle, favorable, and moist breeze, as well as lutes, are likewise praised;
so too are a forehead, a bow, and that which belongs to Indra.
Elsewhere, it is not taught that there is any auspicious or praiseworthy fruit.
The house-lizard (*gṛhagodhikā*) is *chuchu* (or *cchu*); the *piṅgalā* and the female jackal (*śivā*) are *śyāmā*; the *ralā* (crane) is also [so].
In setting out on a journey, those on the left are auspicious.
The female vulture, the bhasa-bhāṣaka,
the piñjala, the aplava, the kambu, the kiṃtsaka, the ruru, and the hawk [are auspicious] when on the right side.
The aspect of the bow-family (Cāpanakula) is auspicious; however,
for the Jāhaka, Saraṭa, and Śaśa families, it yields undesirable results.
The cry of the blue jay, the hare, the monitor lizard, the snake, and the boar is considered auspicious;
however, the cry or sight of monkeys and bears is inauspicious or the reverse.
Deer and birds are auspicious when moving to the right; furthermore, deer are auspicious when their number is odd.
This is the same as for the departure of a king from view, but the opposite applies upon his entry.
One who is habitually provocative,
one who speaks harshly,
one whose servants are alienated, and one who goes to another's wife;
Greedy, lacking allies, addicted to vices, ungrateful, and a breaker of established order—he causes the kingdom to waste away like a hand gnawed by disease.
He betrays trust, is under the sway of anger, is cruel, and is base.
He who is negligent and lacks great learning,
and he who is oppressed by the bodily humors,
is one who is bereft of fortune.
Therefore, when a king possesses the opposite qualities, even such an enemy, upon merely being attacked,
quickly meets with destruction— even if he is great— just as a tree infested by woodworms, its vital functions consumed, falls apart.
Deprived of the majesty of their chosen and excellent kings, lacking in valor, and with their foremost elephants, horses, and warriors rendered powerless, they [follow] the vehicles.
Afflicted by grief, she departed; the armies quickly marched against the enemy force.
In battle,
through the grace of the gods and the twice-born, we—
We shall undoubtedly conquer the enemy force;
for there is this popular proverb regarding military power:
even a very small king destroys a superior army.
The king should destroy the enemy's city when it is afflicted by malefic planets and occupied by inauspicious *diṣṭis* and *viṣṭis*.
The time for marching on a military expedition is exactly the same as that for battle; furthermore, when the ascendants are malefic, one should engage in treacherous warfare.
Birds perched upon the ramparts, facing inward, portend danger from the citizens;
those facing outward portend the destruction of outsiders. The same applies to dogs and their offspring.
When comets, meteors, Saturn, Rāhu, Kīlaka, and Mars enter the solar or lunar disc,
or if a partial halo is seen around the sun or moon in whichever direction there appear ants,
hares, deer, pythons, or crows;
Whether in the city or in the army, wherever the *dayas* enter, from that very place one should cause the enemy's city to be destroyed.
When Rāhu and Ketu are in the constellation of Pātāla, there shall be a cessation of water in the city and the felling of *sāla* trees; this must be performed.
If Mars is situated in the seventh house, or in its own navāṃśa, and is aspected by the Moon's son (Mercury), fire should be offered.
Upon reaching the territory and cities of another, a lord of the earth should not obstruct the property of virtuous deities and the twice-born,
nor their weapons.

One should slay those who are terrified by the [astrological] periods; however, one should enter [the enemy camp] when the lunar day, the day of the week, and the asterism are auspicious, and when one's own army is joyful.
Due to portents such as fires in the cardinal directions, blood, dust, and falls of stones and thunderbolts, as well as earthquakes and other such anomalies,
and because of beasts and birds uttering ominous cries at the conclusion of battle— even if the king has been victorious— it is not auspicious for him.
The beasts and birds are auspicious, the gentle breeze brings delight, and the planets appear clear and distinct.
The rays [of light] have departed in two directions, and the circle of the quarters is devoid of dust.
Even if another [person] were to be deformed,
there would be no victory at the conclusion.
Then the king enjoys happiness free from thorns in his realm, while the enemy [is overcome].
(TY 9.35d) End of the Tikanikāyatra.
